executive_summary: The dominant story of the day is the security incident near the White House, where Secret Service agents shot and killed a gunman in the immediate vicinity of the executive mansion — a serious breach that demands attention regardless of what else fills today's news cycle. While the newsletters cover disparate territory ranging from tennis dominance to recipe content, the Foreign Affairs piece on Ebola's lessons carries an indirect but meaningful resonance with the breaking news: both stories center on institutional response capacity under pressure, specifically whether trained systems and personnel can identify and neutralize threats before they cause catastrophic harm. The Secret Service's swift neutralization of the gunman is precisely the kind of rapid institutional response that Foreign Affairs argues was lacking — or hard-won — during epidemic crises. With no long-form analysis available today to provide deeper context on the White House incident, the Foreign Affairs framework on preparedness and lessons learned becomes the most useful analytical lens through which to understand why institutional vigilance, whether against pathogens or physical threats, remains the connective tissue of national security.

items.headline: Ebola's Lessons: How the WHO Mishandled the Crisis
items.blurb: In a 2015 essay, the science journalist Laurie Garrett traced the response to an outbreak of Ebola that had started the year before—the biggest known outbreak in history—and the enormous problems it had revealed in the world's health infrastructure. For years, "the global response to the rise of new pathogens" had been "limited, uncoordinated, and dysfunctional," Garrett wrote. Poor countries had been "unable to detect new diseases quickly and bring them swiftly under control," and rich countries generally showed "only marginal interest in outbreaks" until the microbes seemed to directly threaten their citizens, at which point they would "hysterically overreact." Global health institutions, meanwhile, were "prone to infighting, and more interested in searching for technological silver bullets than engaging in the hard slog of social mobilization and classic local public health work," Garrett argued. She called on the WHO to reform and for rich countries to better fund pandemic preparedness and other public health initiatives. "The world will get what it pays for," she warned, "and right now, that is not very much."

newsletters.title: Grilled salmon salad with lime, chiles and herbs

items.headline: Grilled Salmon Salad With Lime, Chiles and Herbs
items.blurb: A five-star Melissa Clark recipe, with tender salmon and refreshing greens and a bright dressing animated by lime, fish sauce and herbs? I'm sold. Cook the salmon in the oven if you don't have a grill.

items.headline: Pan-Seared Ranch Chicken
items.blurb: In this smart recipe, Ali Slagle turns to Greek yogurt to make a simple rendition of ranch dressing. Use half of that dressing to marinate the chicken breasts and set aside the other half for serving. It's an herby and cool accompaniment that's also great with green vegetables.

items.headline: Toasted Coconut Rice Salad
items.blurb: Kayla Hoang toasts grains of rice in a skillet before adding water and a can of coconut milk to simmer — a small step with big impact on the flavor of this gingery tofu-topped salad. Cabbage slaw, scallions and cashews add crispness and crunch.

items.headline: Ricotta Pasta Alla Vodka
items.blurb: Eric Kim reaches for ricotta in his version of this retro Italian classic, dolloping the creamy fresh cheese on top of each bowl.

items.headline: Thick Backyard Burgers
items.blurb: If your dinner plans include cooking outdoors, as mine do, then take a look at Kenji López-Alt's guide to making better burgers, then zoom in on this recipe for making beefy burgers on the grill. We've got a video of Kenji making them, too.

items.headline: Making sense of an Alcaraz-less French Open
items.blurb: The French Open will not come down to Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner. At least probably not, given that the tournament starts today at Roland Garros and Alcaraz is not in the draw because of a dreaded wrist injury. Without the two-time defending champion, there's a clear lane for his chief rival. The 24-year-old Sinner will complete the career Grand Slam if he takes care of business against a weakened field. The women's draw is a lot more open, with Iga Świątek and Aryna Sabalenka entering as roughly co-favorites.

items.headline: Knicks-Cavs is looking sweepy
items.blurb: The Knicks are on the verge of their first NBA Finals in 27 years after a 121-108 Game 3 victory in Cleveland, where home support and a certain famous couple didn't make the Cavs seem any less shell-shocked from their Game 1 collapse. Here's your regular reminder that no NBA team has ever blown a 3-0 lead.

items.headline: NHL conference finals thriller
items.blurb: The NHL conference finals meanwhile served up a thriller, with favorites Carolina blowing a third-period lead against Montreal and staring down a familiar narrative until Nikolaj Ehlers fired home.

breaking_digest.narrative:
Secret Service agents shot and killed a gunman near the White House on Saturday, according to officials [1]. The incident marks a serious security breach in the immediate vicinity of the executive mansion, though no further details on casualties or motive have been confirmed. Secret Service personnel responded to the threat and neutralized the attacker [1].

On a lighter note from the arts world, the Cannes Film Festival concluded its awards ceremony Friday evening with 'Fjord' taking home the Palme d'Or, the festival's top prize [2]. The win caps a prominent run at the prestigious French festival for the film.
